paragraphs.heading: A push at right angles
paragraphs.text: When an object touches a surface, a contact force acts between them. The normal force is the part of that contact push that points straight out from the surface, at a right angle to it. Here the word normal is borrowed from geometry, where it means perpendicular, not ordinary. It is usually written F_N.

paragraphs.heading: Why you do not sink
paragraphs.text: Picture someone standing still on a platform. Gravity tugs them toward the centre of the Earth, and something has to push back or they would keep going down. That push back comes from the platform's molecules resisting, and it is the normal force. It is one kind of ground reaction force.

paragraphs.heading: On a table and on a slope
paragraphs.text: For an object sitting on a flat table, the normal force matches its weight in size and points the opposite way, so Fₙ = mg. Here m is the mass and g is the strength of gravity, about 9.81 N/kg on Earth. The table must be strong enough to give this push without breaking. On a slope the push is still perpendicular to the surface, and its size becomes Fₙ = mgcos (θ), where θ is the slope's angle from the horizontal.

paragraphs.heading: Normal force and friction
paragraphs.text: If a person stands on a slope without sliding or sinking, the ground's total push on them splits into two parts. One part is the normal force, at right angles to the ground. The other runs along the ground and is friction.

paragraphs.heading: A common mistake
paragraphs.text: People often assume the normal force and weight are an action and reaction pair, but that is an error. On the table the two must be equal in size to explain why the object does not accelerate upward. A bouncing ball shows the difference: it speeds upward because the normal force on it is bigger than its weight.

paragraphs.heading: What a scale really reads
paragraphs.text: In a lift that is still or moving at a steady speed, the floor pushes up on your feet with a force equal to your weight. When the lift speeds up going upward, that push grows and you feel heavier. When it speeds up going downward, the push shrinks and you feel lighter. A bathroom scale in the lift shows these changes, because it measures the normal force on your feet, not the pull of gravity, which stays the same.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: At the smallest scale the normal force is not a force in its own right. It arises from the Pauli exclusion principle, through the way electrons at the two surfaces interact. The atoms of two surfaces cannot pass into each other without a large amount of energy. Physicists often model this with the van der Waals force, which rises very steeply as the gap closes.
